Nolvex is pleased to submit the enclosed technical and financial proposal for the Combined Dual-System Development Package: Track A, the Automated AI & Data Compliance Platform ("Unified Active Audit"), and Track B, the Agentic AI Back-Office Processor ("Zero-Template Autonomous Operator"). We propose to architect, build, prove and hand over both platforms over the RFP's 24-week, six-phase life cycle, against milestones M1.1 to M6.3, for a fixed professional-services price of KES 3,900,000 (approximately USD 30,233), VAT exclusive. Single-track pricing (Track A: KES 1,800,000; Track B: KES 2,300,000) is given in Section 12 should you prefer to procure one system first.

We have read the RFP as a product thesis rather than a feature list. Its value lies in two things incumbents do not do: intervening in live AI data flows and turning every intervention into regulator-ready evidence; and processing documents nobody has templated while learning from each human correction. Our proposal is organised around proving exactly those differentiators:

  • Measurable, not aspirational. Each differentiator carries an acceptance test the Issuing Organization can run: p99 masking latency under 50 ms at the proxy, evidenced by K6 at every phase gate; field-level extraction accuracy above 95% on a held-out benchmark set you control; and a demonstration that one reviewer correction changes the next extraction without engineering involvement (Section 2.2).
  • Engineered for the hard numbers. A Rust hot path with a per-stage latency budget; a WORM ledger on S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a hash chain and external timestamps; schema-guided vision-language extraction with calibrated per-field confidence; and Temporal durable execution for every document lifecycle (Section 5).
  • Transparent commercially. A fixed price per phase, paid on milestone acceptance exactly as RFP §4 prescribes; an open-source-first stack with no embedded licence fees; itemised pass-through costs; and a predictable post-handover cost model, including a Year-1 total-cost view (Section 12).

Nolvex has also built a working demonstration of both tracks for this response; its screenshots are in Section 5.9, and we offer a live session on your own sample prompts and documents within ten business days of shortlisting (Section 7.3), so that the evaluation can rest on observed behaviour rather than claims.

2.1What we will deliver

Track A — Unified Active Audit
  • A Rust in-line proxy that detects PII/PHI/PCI in streaming LLM prompts and responses and replaces each span with a context-preserving semantic token, so downstream models keep reasoning while the data never leaves your boundary (§5.1–5.2).
  • A WORM audit ledger: Kafka → ClickHouse for query, S3 Object Lock (compliance mode) as the authoritative hash-chained record, with external timestamp anchoring (§5.3).
  • A one-click compliance generator that maps every event to ISO 42001, HIPAA, EU AI Act and SOC 2 controls and exports audit packages as PDF and CSV (§5.3, Appendix F).
  • Live connectors for AWS CloudTrail, Snowflake, OpenAI and Anthropic (M3.1).
Track B — Zero-Template Autonomous Operator
  • A schema-guided vision-language extraction core for unformatted, handwritten and variable-layout documents, with per-field provenance and calibrated confidence (§5.4–5.5).
  • A Temporal.io state machine holding each document's lifecycle durably across retries, timers and human review (§5.7).
  • A closed-loop HITL workbench for fields below 95% confidence whose corrections flow back into exemplar memory, routing rules and thresholds automatically (§5.6, §5.9).
  • A hybrid execution engine: HL7 FHIR R4 (Epic, Oracle Health/Cerner), NetSuite, SFTP, REST and SOAP adapters, with a computer-vision GUI agent as the fallback for legacy software (§5.7).

Both tracks share one platform layer: a multi-tenant admin portal with role-based access control, SAML 2.0 / Okta single sign-on and usage metering (M4.3); Terraform-provisioned Kubernetes on EKS or GKE with GitOps CI/CD (M1.3); SOC 2 and HIPAA audit-readiness evidence, an accredited penetration test with zero unresolved High or Critical findings, and K6/Locust benchmarks (M5.1–M5.3); production rollout, full source and documentation transfer with test coverage above 85%, training and an SLA handover (M6.1–M6.3).

The RFP's thesis is correct, and it is more urgent than it was when the incumbents it names were last evaluated. Below we restate the gap with current, sourced evidence (October 2026), sharpen it where the market has moved, and derive the design principles that shape Sections 5 and 6. Numbered references are listed in Appendix H.

3.2What category leadership requires

Track A — "Intervene on content, prove it with evidence nobody can edit"
  • Content-level, in-line tokenisation with a published, independently reproducible p99 — the number no incumbent publishes.
  • A WORM ledger whose authoritative copy cannot be altered by the operator, the vendor or a cloud root account, verified by a tool the auditor can run themselves.
  • Per-event control mapping across ISO 42001, HIPAA, EU AI Act and SOC 2, exported as a package an auditor can accept — the combination no product ships today[12].
  • Model- and gateway-agnostic by design, so consolidation among guardrail vendors becomes the client's opportunity rather than its risk.
Track B — "Schema, not template; calibrated confidence, not guesswork; learn from every correction"
  • Schema-driven extraction that needs a target data definition and zero layout knowledge — removing the "skill per document type" cost line.
  • Calibrated confidence so that "95%" is a measured probability with a reported error bound on auto-approved fields, not a verbalised score.
  • A closed loop in which a reviewer's correction changes the next extraction the same day, through exemplar retrieval and routing, with no retraining cycle.
  • Durable, verified, audited execution — Temporal orchestration, read-back verification and ledger evidence — the controls whose absence is cancelling agentic projects.

3.3Design principles that follow

  1. Deterministic first, models second, on the hot path. Structured identifiers are resolved by compiled automata in microseconds; statistical models handle only what is ambiguous, inside a hard deadline, with a fail-closed fallback (§5.2).
  2. Evidence is a by-product of operation. The same event that drives the product (a masking decision, a review action, a write-back) is the compliance evidence — never a separate collection job (§5.3).
  3. Every number is defined so it can be audited. Latency is p99 at a named measurement point; accuracy is field-level on a held-out set the client controls; confidence is calibrated and its error reported (§5.5, §5.8).
  4. Human oversight is a feature, not a fallback. The HITL workbench is designed for throughput and produces the human-oversight evidence ISO 42001 and EU AI Act Article 14 require (§5.6, §6).
  5. No lock-in. Open-source-first components, open-weight model fallbacks, provider-agnostic routing, and full IP assignment to the Issuing Organization (§5.10, §12.10).
  6. Trust nobody, including Nolvex. The ledger verifier is open source and runs without access to Nolvex systems; the benchmark test split is held by the client (§5.3, §5.5).

5Technical Proposal

Section 5 describes how each system is built, why the design meets the RFP's hard numbers, and what the Issuing Organization's users will see. Sections 5.1–5.3 cover Track A, 5.4–5.7 cover Track B, 5.8 maps every hard target to a measurement, 5.9 presents interface concept designs and 5.10 the technology stack.

5.1Track A — Unified Active Audit: solution architecture Track A

Track A places a Rust proxy on the request path between client workloads and the connected AI and data services. Each inbound payload passes through a semantic masker that detects PII, PHI and PCI and replaces every sensitive span with a context-preserving token before real-time dispatch to the model; on the response path, tokens echoed by the model are re-hydrated for authorised consumers only. Every decision is emitted as an audit event to Kafka and persisted in a WORM ledger — ClickHouse for query, S3 Object Lock for immutability — from which the compliance generator produces audit packages mapped to ISO 42001, HIPAA, EU AI Act and SOC 2 controls. The hot path never waits for persistence.

Figure 1 — Track A: Unified Active Audit architecture. The proxy resolves most spans deterministically and consults the semantic service only for ambiguous spans inside a hard deadline; audit events leave the hot path through a lock-free channel. The S3 Object Lock ledger, not ClickHouse, is the authoritative record.
ComponentResponsibility and design decisions
Rust proxy / semantic maskerTerminates TLS, authenticates tenant and caller, evaluates the route policy, runs the deterministic detection pass (compiled RegexSet and Aho-Corasick automata, format validators, tenant dictionaries), calls the semantic service only for spans the deterministic pass marks ambiguous, substitutes context-preserving tokens, forwards to the connector, re-hydrates tokens on the response path for authorised consumers and emits an audit event. Stream-aware for chunked LLM responses (§5.2). Stateless; scales horizontally behind a network load balancer.
Python semantic serviceDistilled transformer NER served through ONNX Runtime (int8) plus a zero-shot entity-type head so tenants can add entity types (e.g. "policy number", "DEA number") without retraining; a small contextual embedding model derives each span's semantic role (patient, provider, payer, cardholder) and a quantised context vector used in the token. Micro-batching with a hard deadline; if the deadline is missed the proxy applies the fail-closed policy for that span.
Token vaultToken-to-value mappings held in PostgreSQL with envelope encryption under AWS KMS and a Redis cache for the sub-millisecond hit path. Token identifiers are derived with an HMAC under a per-tenant key so the same value yields the same token within a session (consistent references) but different tokens across sessions (unlinkable). Every lookup is itself an audited event.
KafkaDurable, ordered backbone; topics per event class with tenant-keyed partitions; acks=all; decouples the hot path from persistence and lets ClickHouse and the ledger writer consume independently.
WORM ledger (ClickHouse + S3 Object Lock)ClickHouse ingests through Kafka engine tables for interactive query and dashboards; a ledger writer seals batches, computes a SHA-256 hash chain with Merkle roots and writes them to S3 with Object Lock in compliance mode under a tenant-defined retention. Compliance mode cannot be shortened or deleted by any principal, including the root account, until retention expires (§5.3).
Compliance generator / audit exportMaps each event class to controls in ISO 42001, HIPAA, EU AI Act and SOC 2 (Appendix C), produces one-click PDF and CSV packages per framework, tenant and period, verifies the hash chain before export and embeds the verification result in the package (Appendix F); retention and legal-hold API.
Connectors (M3.1)OpenAI and Anthropic (prompt/response dispatch, streaming, tool-call payload masking); Snowflake (SQL-over-HTTP with result-set masking and query logging); AWS CloudTrail (log ingestion into the ledger with event-class mapping). Each is a Rust crate implementing a common connector trait with contract tests against recorded fixtures.

5.2Semantic tokenization in depth Track A

Masking that breaks the model's ability to reason is not useful; the RFP's phrase "context-preserving" is the design constraint. Nolvex's token carries three things the model needs and nothing it must not have: the entity type, its semantic role in the text and a stable identifier so that references stay consistent throughout a conversation.

Figure 2 — Semantic tokenization, worked example. Clinical content ("atrial fibrillation", "$180") is preserved because it is not an identifier; identifiers are replaced by typed, role-tagged, session-consistent tokens so the model can still resolve "her" to the patient. Unauthorised consumers receive the tokenised response; the card number is never re-hydrated (PCI policy: irreversible). Names are illustrative.

Detection tiers

  1. Deterministic (≤ 5 ms). Compiled RegexSet and Aho-Corasick automata for structured identifiers — card numbers with Luhn validation, SSN and ITIN rules, NPI check digits, MRN patterns per tenant, IBAN, e-mail, phone, dates, IP and device identifiers — plus tenant dictionaries (staff names, locations). Resolves the majority of PCI and structured PHI without any model call.
  2. Statistical NER (≤ 20 ms). A distilled transformer served through ONNX Runtime for PERSON, ORGANIZATION, LOCATION, DATE and health-specific entities, with a zero-shot entity head so tenants can declare new entity types in configuration. Only spans the deterministic tier marks ambiguous (free-text names, addresses) reach this tier.
  3. Contextual embedding (≤ 8 ms, same call). Each detected span is embedded with its surrounding window; nearest-prototype matching assigns the semantic role (patient, provider, payer, guarantor, cardholder) and a quantised context vector that is encoded into the token for downstream disambiguation. The embedding also catches variants the regex tier misses (nicknames, transliterations).

Token design and reversibility

  • Format. ⟦TYPE_n|role⟧, with n assigned in order of first appearance within the session and derived from an HMAC of the canonical value under a per-tenant KMS key, so the same person is always PERSON_1 in that conversation, pronouns resolve, and tokens from different sessions cannot be linked.
  • Format-preserving options per entity type, configured per tenant: dates shifted by a consistent per-session offset (clinical intervals stay correct), ages bucketed, ZIP codes truncated to three digits in line with the HIPAA Safe Harbor method, amounts kept.
  • Reversibility is a policy, not a default. PCI primary account numbers are tokenised irreversibly; PHI tokens are reversible only for consumers whose identity and purpose the route policy authorises; re-hydration events are written to the ledger with the consumer identity.
  • Streaming. Response chunks are scanned with a sliding window; a token that may straddle a chunk boundary is held back (at most the length of a token) until the boundary is resolved, so first-byte latency stays inside the budget and partial tokens are never emitted.
  • Fail-closed. If the semantic tier misses its deadline, the route policy decides per entity class: redact the ambiguous span, or reject the request; the choice and the timeout are recorded.

Proving context preservation. At M2.1 Nolvex delivers a paired-prompt benchmark: the same tasks are run on raw and masked inputs across the client-approved models; structured tasks are scored by exact match and free-text tasks by an LLM judge for answer equivalence. The acceptance target is ≥ 97% equivalence on the agreed task set, reported with the K6 latency results.

5.3WORM ledger and compliance generator in depth Track A

The ledger exists to let an auditor answer "what happened, in what order, and can I trust the record?" without trusting the operator. Three properties deliver that: the ledger never stores secrets, the authoritative copy cannot be altered by anyone, and any alteration or gap is detectable by a verifier that does not need Nolvex.

Figure 3 — Ledger integrity chain. Each sealed batch commits to the previous one; Object Lock compliance mode makes the stored batches immutable; periodic external timestamps prove the chain existed at a point in time; a stand-alone verifier lets the auditor check all of it without trusting the operator.

Compliance generator

  • Control map as versioned data. Each event class (masking decision, re-hydration, policy change, model version change, connector call, access review, backup test, incident) maps to one or more controls in ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A, HIPAA Security Rule §164.308–316, SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria and EU AI Act Articles 9–15. The map is stored in PostgreSQL, editable by the client's compliance owner in the ledger UI, and every change is itself an event. Appendix C shows a sample; the full map is delivered at M1.1.
  • One-click packages. For a framework, tenant and period the generator produces a PDF (cover and attestation page, control coverage matrix, evidence samples per control, exceptions and open items, chain verification result, model and policy inventory) and CSV extracts for the auditor's own tooling. A concept layout is in Appendix F.
  • Operational evidence, continuously. Because evidence is derived from the ledger as events occur, a SOC 2 Type II observation period or an ISO 42001 surveillance audit can be answered for any window after go-live, not reconstructed.
  • Retention and legal hold. Retention per tenant and framework (HIPAA documentation retention of six years is the default for PHI-related events); legal-hold API freezes batches beyond retention; deletion after retention is itself an audited, scheduled operation.

5.4Track B — Zero-Template Autonomous Operator: solution architecture Track B

Track B ingests unstructured documents, extracts structured data with a vision-language model guided only by a target schema (no layout templates), scores every field with a calibrated confidence, routes anything below 95% to the human-in-the-loop workbench, and writes approved records to the system of record through an API adapter or, where none exists, a computer-vision GUI agent. Temporal.io holds each document's lifecycle durably across retries and human-review waits. Reviewer corrections are written back into exemplar memory, routing rules and thresholds so that subsequent similar documents are extracted and routed more accurately — the closed loop the RFP asks for.

Figure 4 — Track B: Zero-Template Autonomous Operator architecture (RFP §2 Track B flow). The confidence evaluator is the gate: fields at or above 95% calibrated confidence auto-approve, anything lower goes to the workbench, and every correction feeds the memory that the extraction core reads on the next document.

5.5Zero-template extraction and calibrated confidence Track B

Extraction without templates

  1. Document-class detection. The VLM classifies each page set against the client's class catalogue (e.g. freight bill of lading, prior-authorisation request, supporting clinical notes) zero-shot; unknown classes route to the workbench for a one-time schema assignment rather than failing.
  2. Schema-guided prompting. Each class has a target JSON Schema (fields, types, enumerations, required flags, cross-field rules) defined with the client at M1.1. The schema, not a layout, drives the prompt; the model is asked to return a typed object with, for every field, the page and bounding box it was read from. Structured-output decoding guarantees schema-valid JSON.
  3. Exemplar retrieval. Before extraction, the page embedding is matched (pgvector, HNSW) against the active-learning memory; the nearest previously-corrected documents are included as few-shot exemplars. This is how one correction improves the next similar document without any model retraining.
  4. OCR cross-check and self-consistency. Numeric and identifier fields (totals, dates, NPI, member IDs, container numbers) are cross-checked against an independent OCR pass; critical fields are sampled multiple times and must agree. Disagreement lowers confidence rather than silently picking an answer.
  5. Handwriting. The VLM reads handwritten content directly; because OCR agreement is weaker on handwriting, the calibration model learns to weight it accordingly, so handwritten fields start with more human review and need less as exemplars accumulate.
  6. Validation. Business rules from the schema (line items reconcile to totals, dates in range, codes in reference lists such as ICD-10, CPT, HCPCS, UN/LOCODE) run before scoring; a rule failure is a strong negative feature.

Calibrated confidence — why "95%" must mean 95%

A model's verbalised confidence is not a probability; using it as one would make the RFP's 95% threshold meaningless. Nolvex therefore computes a calibrated probability per field from observable features — agreement across sampled extractions, agreement with OCR, validator and business-rule outcomes, similarity to retrieved exemplars, document-quality metrics and, where the model exposes them, token log-probabilities — fitted with isotonic regression on the held-out calibration split of the benchmark set. The 95% gate is applied to that calibrated probability. Reported metrics include per-class accuracy, auto-approval rate, precision of auto-approved fields and expected calibration error (target ≤ 0.05), re-fitted nightly from reviewer outcomes so that drift in document mix or model behaviour is caught by the harness, not by customers.

Accuracy, defined so it can be audited

Field-level exact-match accuracy after normalisation (whitespace, case, date and number formats) across required fields on a stratified benchmark of at least 300 labelled documents per class, split 60/20/20 into tuning, calibration and held-out test; the test split is never used for prompt tuning, exemplar selection or calibration. The RFP's "> 95% accuracy on unformatted documents" is measured on that held-out split at M2.2 and re-validated at M4.1 and M5.3.

5.6Closed-loop HITL and active learning Track B

The workbench (concept design in §5.9, Figure 7) is where the RFP's "active learning" becomes mechanical rather than aspirational. A reviewer sees the document and the extracted fields side by side, with each low-confidence field highlighted at its source location; they correct, annotate or approve with the keyboard; and one action — "approve and retrain" — triggers the feedback loop below.

Feedback channelWhat is written backEffect on the next document
Exemplar memoryThe corrected document (page embedding, final field values, bounding boxes, reviewer notes) is stored as a retrievable exemplar, stamped with model version and prompt hash.Similar layouts retrieve the exemplar as a few-shot example; the same mistake is not repeated.
Routing rulesPer-class statistics update: which prompt variant, model or pre-processing profile yields the best accuracy for that class and quality band.Documents of that class are routed to the best-performing configuration automatically.
Threshold re-calibrationReviewer outcomes (accepted vs corrected) become labels for the calibration model; nightly re-fit per class.The 95% gate tracks real-world precision; auto-approval rate rises as the loop matures.
Validator suggestionsRepeated corrections of the same shape (e.g. a date format, a code list) are surfaced as proposed rules for the client's analyst to accept.Systematic errors are caught deterministically rather than by review.
Evaluation set growthA sampled fraction of corrected documents is added to the benchmark (never to the held-out test split).The nightly harness measures real production distribution, not only the original sample.
  • Reviewer quality. Golden documents with known answers are injected into queues at a low rate; reviewer agreement and golden accuracy are reported in the admin console; two-person review can be required per class.
  • Queues and SLAs. Priority by business deadline (e.g. prior-authorisation decision windows), skill-based assignment, SLA timers held by Temporal, escalation on breach.
  • Auditability. Every review action is an event in the Track A ledger with reviewer identity, before/after values and timing — which is also the human-oversight evidence ISO 42001 and EU AI Act Article 14 ask for.
  • Optional fine-tuning. Once corrections per class exceed a few thousand, supervised fine-tuning (LoRA) of an open-weight VLM in the client's cloud becomes worthwhile; it is available as an add-on (§12.8) and is not required to meet the RFP targets.

5.7Temporal state machine and hybrid execution engine Track B

Figure 5 — Document lifecycle state machine (Temporal workflow). Each transition is a durable activity with its own retry policy; human review is a signal-awaited state with an SLA timer; a failed read-back verification runs the adapter's compensation path and parks the document in the exception queue.
  • One workflow per document, with page-level child activities for parallelism; idempotent activities keyed by document and attempt so retries never double-write; worker pools sized per activity type (CPU for pre-processing, API-bound for VLM calls, I/O-bound for adapters).
  • Redis execution queue. Intake bursts (e.g. a morning SFTP drop of thousands of files) are absorbed by a Redis-backed queue that releases work into Temporal at the configured rate, protecting VLM API quotas and keeping the 1,000 docs/hour throughput steady rather than spiky.
  • Deployment. Self-hosted Temporal on Kubernetes with PostgreSQL persistence in the client's account; Temporal Cloud is available as a pass-through option where the client prefers managed operation.

Hybrid execution engine — write-back adapters (M3.2)

Every adapter implements one contract — validate → map → commit → verify → compensate — so that the workflow treats a FHIR server, an ERP and a legacy screen identically: it only ever asks "did the record land, and can I read it back?"

TargetApproachRealities designed for
Epic and Oracle Health (Cerner) — HL7 FHIR R4SMART Backend Services authorisation (client-credentials with a signed JWT against the registered key); FHIR R4 resources inside each vendor's documented write surface — on Epic, DocumentReference create/update, Observation (vitals/flowsheets) create, MedicationRequest/ServiceRequest update for prior authorisation, and Claim $submit/$inquire with $submit-attachment for Da Vinci PAS; on Oracle Health, POST/PUT on DocumentReference and system-scope writes on Observation, Condition, AllergyIntolerance, Appointment and MedicationRequest[69][70]; conditional create with client-generated identifiers for idempotency; read-back verification.Every write is enabled per resource, per customer: Epic requires the health system's open.epic subscription and a client-record download per environment, Oracle Health requires tenant provisioning through its developer programme[69][70]. Registrations are started in week 1 (D-5); resource-level write support is confirmed in the sandbox at M1.1 and the adapter is scoped to what the client's instance permits (A-2). Prior-authorisation submission to payers follows the HL7 Da Vinci PAS profile that CMS recommends for the FHIR Prior Authorization APIs due 1 January 2027 (§6.1).
NetSuiteSuiteTalk REST record and query (SuiteQL) services with OAuth 2.0 client-credentials (certificate-based machine-to-machine) — not token-based authentication, which NetSuite closes to new integrations from release 2027.1, and not SOAP, which is being sunset[73]; external-id keys for idempotent upserts; transformation rules in a declarative mapping DSL; sandbox-first testing.Custom fields and record types differ per account; the mapping DSL is client-editable without code changes.
SFTP and database syncSFTP drops with checksum manifests and optional PGP; database upserts through SQLAlchemy with explicit transaction boundaries.Partner file specifications (CSV, XML, EDI) change; schema versioning per partner.
Generic REST and SOAPAdapters generated from OpenAPI and WSDL definitions, with the same mapping DSL, retry and verification stages.Authentication schemes vary; secrets are injected from Vault / Secrets Manager (§6.4).

Computer-vision GUI fallback agent (M3.3)

  • Deterministic first, vision second. Where the target is a web application, recorded Playwright flows using accessibility roles and stable selectors execute the common path; the vision-language model is invoked only to ground an element when selectors fail (set-of-marks screenshot prompting) or to confirm state. For desktop applications a Windows runner uses the UI Automation tree before falling back to pixel-level control.
  • Every action verified. Each step is followed by a screenshot assertion of the expected state; the final record is read back from the screen and compared with the approved data before the workflow marks the document written.
  • Guard-rails. Allow-listed applications, screens and fields; dry-run mode that produces an action plan without executing; change detection (layout drift beyond a threshold) that diverts the document to the exception queue rather than guessing; full screen recording attached to the ledger event.

5.8How each hard target will be met Both tracks

Each RFP target below has a definition, a measurement method, a tool, a milestone at which the number is delivered, and the external evidence that makes the design credible before Nolvex has measured anything. Where public evidence does not support a claim, we say so and show how the design still meets the RFP's intent.

5.8.1 Sub-50 ms semantic masking (Track A, M2.1)

The target is a p99 of 50 ms measured at the proxy for the masking stage, excluding upstream LLM time, under the RFP's 5,000 req/s load. The budget is allocated per stage and enforced by nightly K6 runs from Phase 2.

Figure 6 — Latency budget by stage. Audit emission is not on the path at all; it leaves through a lock-free channel after the response is forwarded.
StageBudget (p99)Technique
TLS, parsing, tenant auth≤ 3 msTokio/Hyper async runtime; zero-copy bodies; cached authorisation decisions; connection pooling to connectors.
Deterministic detection≤ 5 msCompiled RegexSet / Aho-Corasick; format validators (Luhn, SSN, NPI, IBAN, MRN patterns); dictionary tries. Resolves most PCI and structured PHI without a model call.
Semantic detection and tokenization≤ 28 msDistilled token-classification NER (int8, ONNX Runtime) and a small embedding model served over gRPC with micro-batching; Redis token-cache hit path < 1 ms; hard deadline with policy-defined fail-closed behaviour. Zero-shot entity types for tenant-defined classes run on a GPU-served replica under the same deadline.
Rewrite and emit≤ 5 msIn-place span replacement; audit event handed to a lock-free channel and flushed to Kafka asynchronously, never on the request path.
Headroom≈ 9 msScheduling jitter and network variance; CPU requests sized to avoid CFS throttling, which is the usual cause of p99 cliffs in containerised proxies.
Why this budget is credible — independent evidence
  • Presidio-class detection (regex, checksums and a spaCy NER) measures a median of 15 ms per request on a laptop CPU in an independent June 2026 benchmark[22]; a quantised DistilBERT-class classifier on a 4-vCPU cloud instance delivers p95 under 28 ms at sequence length 128 with int8 ONNX Runtime[23]. Those are the components inside Nolvex's 28 ms semantic budget.
  • Zero-shot NER of the GLiNER class costs 160–200 ms on CPU[22], and external PII APIs cost hundreds of milliseconds[50]. That is why neither is on Nolvex's CPU hot path: zero-shot types are GPU-served, and no external service is ever called in-line.
  • Rust proxies set the performance reference: Cloudflare's Pingora reduced p95 time-to-first-byte by 80 ms and CPU by about 70% against NGINX at over one trillion requests per day[27], and Rust frameworks lead the TechEmpower Round 23 benchmarks[28].
  • No vendor publishes an independently verified sub-50 ms tokenisation p99; published vendor medians cluster around 30–65 ms[50]. Nolvex's design is the configuration consistent with the component evidence at 5,000 req/s, and it is proven with K6 at M2.1 rather than asserted.

Streaming responses are re-hydrated per chunk with a sliding window so the first byte is not delayed beyond the budget. Context preservation is verified by the paired-prompt benchmark in §5.2 — an approach supported by peer-reviewed findings that typed, instance-indexed, reversible placeholders preserve LLM task quality far better than irreversible redaction[25][26].

5.8.2 Greater than 95% extraction accuracy (Track B, M2.2)

Nolvex commits to a three-part definition so that the number means what the RFP intends and can be audited:

MetricCommitmentMeasured how
End-to-end accuracy of delivered records (auto-approved plus reviewed fields)> 95%Field-level exact match after normalisation on the held-out test split, per class and quality band, at M2.2, M4.1 and M5.3.
Precision of auto-approved fields (those passing the 95% gate)≥ 97%Calibrated threshold with reported expected calibration error ≤ 0.05; auto-approval coverage reported alongside so that precision cannot be bought by routing everything to review.
Raw model accuracy before reviewReported, not gatedPer class and quality band (clean, scanned, handwritten); drives routing and threshold decisions and shows the loop improving over time.
  • Benchmark set. At least 300 labelled documents per class, stratified by quality, split 60/20/20 for tuning, calibration and held-out testing; the test split is held by the client and never used for tuning (A-5).
  • Method. Schema-guided prompting with retrieved exemplars; OCR cross-check on numeric and identifier fields; self-consistency on critical fields; business-rule validation; calibrated routing (§5.5).
  • What the evidence supports. Calibrated, feature-based confidence with conformal-style thresholds is now the published state of the art for this exact problem: one 2026 study reports 99.1% accuracy at 80% auto-approval coverage after recalibration[40]; another auto-approves 49–72% of fields at a 10% error budget where native model confidence manages under 7%[39]; and the ConfBench evaluation shows that first-token log-probabilities with OCR-plus-image input give the best confidence signal while verbalised confidence is poorly calibrated[37][38]. Nolvex's evaluator is built on those findings.
  • Handwriting, stated honestly. No public benchmark supports 95% accuracy on free-text handwritten narrative: the best model on the 2026 WildHandBench scores 71.9% against a human 77.1%[36], and on handwritten medical forms current models reach about 85–90% on discrete fields while free-text narrative remains error-prone[35]. Nolvex therefore treats handwritten discrete fields (dates, identifiers, codes, amounts, check-boxes) as in-gate, strengthened by validators and exemplars, and routes handwritten narrative fields to review by default, with their accuracy reported separately. End-to-end delivered accuracy above 95% is maintained because those fields are human-verified; the RFP's intent — no templates, handwriting handled, humans only where needed — is met without a claim the evidence cannot support.
  • Model choice. On the OmniDocBench v1.6 leaderboard (Sep 2026) specialist open-weight document models such as PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 and MinerU2.5-Pro score above the frontier API models[33], so the open-weight fallback in A-4 is a peer, not a compromise. Candidate API models current at the time of writing are listed in §5.10; the selection is fixed at M1.1 against the benchmark.

5.8.3 Load targets — 5,000 req/s (Track A) and 1,000 docs/hr (Track B), M5.3

  • Track A. Stateless proxy behind a network load balancer; sizing assumes 1,000–1,500 req/s per 2-vCPU pod, so 4–6 pods plus one spare meet the target with the semantic service scaled independently. Kafka audit topic with ≥ 12 partitions; ClickHouse ingestion through the Kafka engine or ClickPipes, which sustain tens of thousands of events per second per replica[29]; S3 absorbs at least 3,500 PUTs per second per prefix[30], far above the ledger writer's batch rate. K6 runs 1.5× target (7,500 req/s) for 30 minutes with p99 within budget and zero event loss.
  • Track B. 1,000 docs/hr is roughly 17 per minute, or about 70 pages per minute at four pages per document; concurrency is bounded by VLM API limits, so the workflow applies a token-bucket limiter, page-level parallelism and batching, with the Redis queue absorbing bursts. Locust drives a 2,000-document synthetic corpus over two hours, including HITL routing at the expected rate. At current API prices (input-token cost of roughly USD 0.0002–0.005 per page across the candidate models[47]) Nolvex budgets USD 0.01–0.05 per document all-in, refined at M1.3 — so throughput is an engineering question, not a cost barrier. An open-weight VLM on client GPU capacity is the documented fallback if API quotas are insufficient (A-4).
  • Orchestration headroom. Temporal's own published figures show sustained spikes above 150,000 actions per second on its cloud service[41]; a self-hosted cluster sized for a few hundred documents in flight has orders of magnitude of headroom.

5.8.4 Greater than 85% test coverage (M6.2)

Coverage is measured per repository with cargo-llvm-cov (Rust), coverage.py (Python) and vitest coverage (TypeScript), reported on every pull request and enforced with a merge gate at 85% line coverage from Phase 2. It includes unit, integration (Testcontainers for Kafka, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, Redis, Temporal, MinIO) and contract tests for every connector and adapter (§8).

5.9User interface — screenshots from the Nolvex demonstration build Both tracks

The RFP asks for a React/Vite HITL interface, a WORM-ledger interface with one-click export and a multi-tenant admin portal. Rather than mock-ups, the figures below are screenshots of a working demonstration build Nolvex assembled for this response: a React 19 / Vite front end over a Python service that implements the three-tier masking engine, session-consistent tokenization, the hash-chained ledger with an independent verifier and one-click evidence packages, zero-shot document classification, template-free schema-guided extraction over a real OCR pass, calibrated-style confidence with the 95% gate, the review workbench and the exemplar memory that changes the next extraction after a correction. Every number on these screens was produced by that build on 23 October 2026 on synthetic documents and prompts (no client data). The build is the basis of the proof-of-capability session offered in §7.3 and will be shown live.

Scope of the demonstration build: it runs the masking engine in Python rather than Rust (latencies shown are its own, measured per request), keeps state in process rather than in Kafka, ClickHouse, Temporal and S3 Object Lock, and used its offline OCR provider for extraction in these captures; a vision-language-model provider (Anthropic, Google or an open-weight model) plugs into the same interface with OCR as the cross-check. The admin console's other tenants are illustrative; the Meridian Health row shows the live counters. 6Security and Compliance Approach

Both systems are built so that the Issuing Organization can evidence controls under SOC 2 (Type II readiness), HIPAA and ISO/IEC 42001, and so that Track A's compliance generator can map events to those frameworks and to the EU AI Act. Nolvex does not itself hold these certifications and claims none; the deliverable is a system whose controls, documentation and evidence support the client's own audits. The regulatory picture below is current as of 22 October 2026 and is the baseline for the control map delivered at M1.1 and verified at M5.1 (sources in Appendix H).

6.1The regulatory landscape this platform must evidence (October 2026)

FrameworkStatus at the time of writingWhat it means for the delivered platforms
EU AI Act (Reg. (EU) 2024/1689, as amended)The "Digital Omnibus on AI" was adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and entered into force on 27 July 2026. Annex III high-risk obligations (Articles 9–15, 17) now apply from 2 December 2027 (previously 2 August 2026); Annex I product-embedded systems from 2 August 2028; synthetic-content marking under Article 50(2) from 2 December 2026. GPAI obligations have applied since August 2025 and the Commission's fining powers since 2 August 2026. The first harmonised standard, EN 18286:2026 (quality management systems for Article 17), was cited in the Official Journal on 14 October 2026; logging, oversight and robustness standards are still in drafting. Penalties reach EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover for prohibited practices and EUR 15 million or 3% for most operator obligations[51][52][54][55].Track B deployments that evaluate eligibility for healthcare services or support insurance decisions may fall within Annex III depending on use; the control map therefore covers Articles 9 (risk management), 10 (data governance), 11 and Annex IV (technical documentation), 12 (record-keeping), 13 (transparency), 14 (human oversight), 15 (accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity) and 17 (QMS), so that the client's customers can evidence them from the ledger ahead of the December 2027 date. The Annex IV documentation pack is an optional add-on (§12.8). The control map is versioned data, so the amended timeline and future harmonised standards are absorbed without code change (R13).
HIPAA Security and Privacy RulesThe current Security Rule remains law. HHS's January 2025 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to strengthen it — mandatory encryption and MFA, an ePHI asset inventory and network map, restoration of critical systems within 72 hours, annual compliance audits, vulnerability scans every six months and annual penetration tests — is not final; HHS's spring 2026 agenda moved the target to July 2027[56][57]. The 2024 reproductive-health privacy rule was vacated nationally in June 2025[58].Nolvex builds to the proposed rule now, so that nothing needs re-engineering when it is finalised: encryption in transit and at rest everywhere, MFA through SSO, an automatically maintained inventory of ePHI data flows (the connector and adapter registry), documented 72-hour restoration demonstrated at M5.1, and six-monthly scanning and annual penetration testing written into the SLA (§12.6). Business Associate Agreements with providers remain the client's responsibility (A-6).
ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (AI management systems)Published December 2023; supplemented by ISO/IEC 42005:2025 (AI system impact assessment, May 2025) and ISO/IEC 42006:2025 (requirements for certification bodies, July 2025). Accredited certification is now available (ANAB-accredited certifiers since September 2024; BSI became the first UKAS-accredited body in November 2025); Anthropic, AWS and Microsoft hold certificates[59][60][61].The platforms produce the artefacts an ISO 42001 audit asks for: AI system inventory and model cards (A.4, A.6.2.7), impact assessments per 42005 (6.1.4, A.5), operation and monitoring (A.6.2.6), recording of event logs (A.6.2.8), responsible-use and intended-use statements (A.9), and third-party model governance (A.10). Appendix C maps each to a system feature and evidence.
SOC 2 (AICPA Trust Services Criteria)The criteria remain the 2017 TSC with the 2022 revised points of focus; a Type II report covers operating effectiveness over a period, typically 6–12 months. AICPA's 2026 activity focuses on audit quality rather than new criteria[62].Because evidence is derived continuously from the ledger, the observation window can start at go-live; M5.1 delivers the control-by-control evidence index for Security, Availability, Processing Integrity and Confidentiality criteria.
NIST AI RMF 1.0 and AI 600-1; NIST CSF 2.0Voluntary frameworks widely referenced by US buyers; NIST states the AI RMF is being revised in 2026[63].The control map includes a crosswalk to the AI RMF functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) so that US customers asking for NIST alignment receive the same evidence packages.

Texas TRAIGA has applied since 1 January 2026[65]; California's CCPA automated decision-making regulations took effect 1 January 2026 with compliance due 1 January 2027[66]; New York's RAISE Act takes effect 1 January 2027[67].Track B's prior-authorisation and similar workflows are consequential decisions under these laws; the HITL workbench, reviewer records and ledger supply the human-review and record-keeping evidence, and the decision explanation stored per document supports adverse-decision disclosure.
CMS-0057-F (Interoperability and Prior Authorization)Decision time frames (72 hours expedited, 7 calendar days standard) and public prior-authorisation metrics have applied since 1 January 2026; the FHIR Prior Authorization, Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs are due 1 January 2027. CMS recommends, but does not require, the HL7 Da Vinci CRD, DTR and PAS implementation guides. Around 53 health plans separately pledged a FHIR electronic prior-authorisation framework by 2027[68][75].Track B's prior-authorisation class is designed around these time frames (SLA timers in Temporal) and the Da Vinci PAS profile for payer submission where supported, which is the write-back path that becomes standard in 2027.

6.3Data protection, residency and threat model

  • Data classification. Four classes (public, internal, confidential, regulated: PII/PHI/PCI) with handling rules enforced in code: regulated data never appears in logs, traces, error messages or the ledger (token identifiers and counts only), and never leaves the client's region un-tokenised.
  • Residency. All stores (Kafka, ClickHouse, S3, PostgreSQL, Redis, Temporal) are deployed in client-selected regions. No data leaves those regions except calls to client-approved model APIs, which are documented with endpoint regions and data categories sent; semantic tokenisation is applied before any payload reaches an external model. Residency constraints are captured at M1.1 and verified at M5.1.
  • Threat model. Delivered at M1.1 using STRIDE per trust boundary (client workload → proxy, proxy → semantic service, proxy → connector, workflow → adapter, GUI agent → legacy application, user → workbench and portal), with abuse cases specific to this product: prompt-injection attempts to exfiltrate tokens, re-hydration by an unauthorised consumer, poisoning of the active-learning memory through malicious corrections, and GUI-agent manipulation by a changed screen. Each has a named control and a test.
  • Tenant isolation. Row-level security on every table; per-tenant KMS keys for the token vault; per-tenant Kafka partition keys and S3 prefixes; isolation tests in CI.
  • PCI scope reduction. Primary account numbers are tokenised irreversibly at the proxy and never stored, keeping downstream systems out of PCI DSS scope.

6.4Secrets management

  • All credentials (connector keys, model API keys, FHIR client certificates, NetSuite OAuth client credentials, SFTP keys, SAML signing keys) are held in AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault and injected at runtime; none are stored in repositories, images or workflow payloads.
  • Encryption keys in AWS KMS with rotation and separate keys per environment and tenant; S3 ledger objects use SSE-KMS; token-vault columns are envelope-encrypted.
  • Workload identity (IRSA / Workload Identity) instead of long-lived cloud keys; secret access is itself written to the ledger.
  • Pre-commit and CI secret scanning (gitleaks); signed commits; dependency pinning.

6.5Penetration testing approach (M5.2)

  • Continuous automated scanning throughout the build: Trivy (images, dependencies), Semgrep, OWASP ZAP baseline against the workbench, admin portal and APIs; findings triaged weekly.
  • An accredited third-party penetration test (CREST or equivalent) in Phase 5, week 17, commissioned by the client or by Nolvex as a pass-through (§12.5). Scope: external and internal network, web applications, APIs (proxy, export, workflow, admin), SAML/SSO flow, cloud configuration review, and product-specific abuse cases from the threat model (token exfiltration via prompt injection, unauthorised re-hydration, memory poisoning).
  • Nolvex remediates all High and Critical findings and obtains a signed re-test confirmation from the auditor before M5.2 acceptance; Medium and Low findings are remediated or risk-accepted by the client in writing.

6.6Additional controls and Nolvex's engagement posture

  • Application security: input validation at every boundary; parameterised queries; CSP and CSRF protection; rate limiting; output encoding in the workbench; dependency and container scanning on every build.
  • Supply chain: pinned dependencies; CycloneDX SBOM per release; cosign-signed images; provenance attestations from CI.
  • Backup and recovery: documented RPO/RTO per store; ledger recovery from S3 and PostgreSQL point-in-time restore demonstrated at M5.1 within the 72-hour window the proposed HIPAA rule would require.
  • Incident response: runbooks for data-exposure, availability and integrity incidents; breach-notification timelines aligned to HIPAA and the client's contracts; post-incident reviews feed the risk register.
  • Nolvex's own posture for this engagement: Nolvex personnel sign confidentiality undertakings; all work is performed in client-controlled environments with MFA and least-privilege access granted by the client (A-7); no client data is stored on Nolvex systems; access is revoked at handover and confirmed in writing.

Figure 12 — Likelihood × impact heat map. Scores are the product L × I; cell shading follows the score bands in the legend.

Reading the map

Two risks sit in the high band (R1 accuracy on hard classes, R3 sandbox access) and four in the elevated band (R2, R4, R6, R11, R14 at 9–12). Each has a Phase 1 action that reduces it before Phase 2 begins: the stratified benchmark and accuracy definition (R1), the access request pack sent at kick-off with fixture-based fallbacks (R3), the per-stage latency budget enforced nightly (R2), the frozen scope baseline and change process (R6), and model pinning with a routing layer that allows swaps (R14). Residual scores are expected to fall to the moderate band by the end of Phase 1 and are re-scored at every phase gate.

Risks the Issuing Organization controls (R3, R9, R11, R12) are listed with the dependency date in §11 so that the mitigation is a calendar entry, not a hope.

10.2Continuity, surge capacity and working model

  • Continuity. A named deputy per role, including the Project Lead, is confirmed at kick-off; documented architecture and ADRs, pairing on critical components and shared ownership of the CI gates reduce key-person risk (R7).
  • Surge capacity. For Phase 4 (three parallel UI and ledger workstreams) and Phase 5 (UAT and remediation) Nolvex can add a second frontend engineer and a QA engineer from its bench at no change to the fixed price; the effort table in §12.4 is the planning basis, not a cap on what Nolvex will deploy to meet a milestone.
  • Working hours. The team works from Nairobi (EAT, UTC+3). A guaranteed overlap window of 3:00–6:00 pm EAT (8:00–11:00 am EST) is held daily for client meetings, decisions and support; extended overlap is arranged for UAT (weeks 17–20) and production rollout (weeks 21–24), including on-call cover in the client's change windows.
  • Channels. Shared Slack or Teams channel; weekly written status report; fortnightly steering meeting; phase-gate reviews; shared backlog and decision log (§7.4).
  • Escalation. Project Lead → Nolvex Director (the same person on this engagement) → named deputy; client escalation path agreed at kick-off.

12.9Payment terms

  • Invoicing. Each phase is invoiced on acceptance of its final milestone (§12.3). Pass-through costs are invoiced monthly in arrears with supporting supplier invoices.
  • Terms. Net 15 days from invoice date.
  • Retention. 10% of each phase payment is held by the client until written phase sign-off, then released with the next invoice (or within 15 days of final sign-off for Phase 6).
  • VAT. 16% VAT applies where applicable and is shown separately on each invoice. All prices in this proposal are VAT exclusive.
  • Currency. Invoices are issued in KES. Payments made in foreign currency are converted at the Central Bank of Kenya indicative rate on the invoice date; bank charges on inbound foreign transfers are borne by the payer.
  • Payment methods. Bank transfer; account details are provided on each invoice.
  • Late payment. Work on the next phase may be paused if an accepted-milestone invoice is more than 15 days overdue; the schedule shifts by the duration of the pause.

12.10Commercial terms

  • Intellectual property. All deliverables developed under this engagement (source code, IaC, documentation, prompts, schemas, exemplar data, control maps, calibration models and any models fine-tuned on client data) are assigned to the client on receipt of final payment; until then the client holds a licence for evaluation, UAT and production use. Open-source components remain under their own licences (§5.10, SBOM). Nolvex retains the right to reuse generic, non-client-specific tooling and know-how.
  • Warranty. 90 days from production deployment (M6.1). Defects in the delivered scope are corrected at no charge, including re-testing. Excluded: defects caused by client changes to code or infrastructure, third-party service changes, or use outside documented limits.
  • Change requests. Scope outside the RFP and this proposal is handled by a written change request stating the change, schedule and price impact, and acceptance criteria; priced at the add-on rates in §12.8 where applicable, otherwise at a blended rate of KES 4,500 per hour; client sign-off before work starts.
  • Confidentiality. Mutual non-disclosure covering client data, systems and this proposal; Nolvex personnel sign confidentiality undertakings; client data is processed only in client-controlled environments (A-7).
  • Acceptance. Per Appendix A and Assumption A-9.
  • Termination. Either party may terminate for uncured material breach on 30 days' written notice; the client may terminate for convenience at any phase gate, paying for accepted milestones and work in progress at the blended rate; deliverables to date are handed over.
  • Liability. Nolvex's aggregate liability is limited to fees paid under the contract; neither party is liable for indirect or consequential loss. Subject to contract negotiation
  • Governing law. Laws of Kenya unless otherwise agreed in the contract. Subject to contract negotiation

BGlossary

TermDefinition
Unified Active AuditTrack A: the proxy, semantic tokenization, event and WORM-ledger platform described in §5.1–5.3 (RFP §1 System #1).
Zero-Template Autonomous OperatorTrack B: the template-free document extraction, HITL and write-back platform described in §5.4–5.7 (RFP §1 System #2).
Semantic tokenizationReplacement of a sensitive value with a token encoding its entity type, semantic role and a session-consistent identifier so that downstream models retain reasoning capability; reversible only for authorised consumers.
PII / PHI / PCIPersonally identifiable information; protected health information; payment-card information.
WORMWrite-once-read-many storage; implemented with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode as the authoritative copy and an append-only ClickHouse store for query.
Hash chain / Merkle rootEach ledger batch records the SHA-256 digest of the previous batch and a Merkle root of its events so that modification, deletion or re-ordering is detectable.
RFC 3161 timestampA signed time-stamp token from a trusted authority proving that a hash existed at a point in time; used to anchor the chain head.
VLMVision-language model: accepts page images and text prompts and returns structured text.
Calibrated confidenceA probability per field, fitted on held-out data, that a value is correct; the 95% gate is applied to this probability, and its error (expected calibration error) is reported.
HITLHuman-in-the-loop: reviewer intervention on fields below the 95% confidence threshold.
Active learningAutomatic feeding of reviewer corrections into prompt exemplars, routing rules and thresholds.
STPStraight-through processing: documents completed without any human touch.
Temporal.ioDurable-execution workflow engine used for the Track B state machine and retry logic.
FHIR / HL7 / Da Vinci PASFast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, the HL7 API standard used for Epic and Oracle Health write-back; Da Vinci PAS is the HL7 implementation guide for prior-authorisation submission.
RBAC / SSO / SAML 2.0Role-based access control; single sign-on; the federation standard used with Okta for the admin portal.
p9999th-percentile value of a latency distribution.
SBOMSoftware bill of materials listing all components and versions in a release.
Pass-throughA cost invoiced at supplier price without margin, or paid directly by the client.
EAT / ESTEast Africa Time (UTC+3) / US Eastern Standard Time (UTC−5).

GAPI contract excerpt (OpenAPI 3.0, illustrative)

An excerpt of the style of contract delivered at M1.1 for the Track A guardrail endpoint and the Track B document endpoint. Full contracts are lint-clean (Spectral) and versioned with breaking-change checks (buf for gRPC).

# Track A — guardrail proxy (excerpt)
paths:
  /v1/guard/chat:
    post:
      summary: Mask and dispatch a chat completion to the route's upstream model
      parameters:
        - { name: X-Tenant-Id, in: header, required: true, schema: { type: string } }
        - { name: X-Route, in: header, required: true, schema: { type: string, example: anthropic-prod } }
        - { name: X-Consumer-Purpose, in: header, required: false, schema: { type: string } }
      requestBody: { $ref: '#/components/requestBodies/ChatRequest' }   # provider-shaped body passes through
      responses:
        '200': { description: Upstream response, re-hydrated if the caller is authorised; SSE when stream=true }
        '422': { description: Blocked by policy (fail-closed or entity class set to block) }
        '504': { description: Semantic stage missed its deadline and the route policy is reject }
      x-nolvex-sla: { masking_p99_ms: 50, measured_at: proxy, excludes: upstream }
      x-nolvex-audit: { event_class: mask.decision, controls: [ISO42001:A.6.2.8, HIPAA:164.312(b), SOC2:CC7.2, EUAIA:Art12] }

# Track B — document intake (excerpt)
  /v1/documents:
    post:
      summary: Submit a document for template-free extraction and downstream write-back
      requestBody:
        content:
          multipart/form-data:
            schema:
              properties:
                file:          { type: string, format: binary }
                schema_id:     { type: string, nullable: true, description: Omit to auto-detect the document class }
                priority:      { type: string, enum: [expedited, standard], default: standard }
                target:        { type: string, enum: [fhir-epic, fhir-oracle, netsuite, sftp, rest, soap, gui], nullable: true }
      responses:
        '202': { description: Accepted; returns workflow_id and a status URL }
  /v1/documents/{workflow_id}:
    get:
      responses:
        '200':
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                properties:
                  state:   { type: string, enum: [INGESTED, PREPROCESSED, EXTRACTED, SCORED, IN_REVIEW, APPROVED, WRITTEN_BACK, VERIFIED, DONE, EXCEPTION] }
                  fields:  { type: array, items: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/ExtractedField' } }
components:
  schemas:
    ExtractedField:
      properties:
        name:        { type: string }
        value:       { }
        confidence:  { type: number, minimum: 0, maximum: 1, description: Calibrated probability the value is correct }
        provenance:  { type: object, properties: { page: { type: integer }, bbox: { type: array, items: { type: number }, minItems: 4, maxItems: 4 } } }
        decision:    { type: string, enum: [auto_approved, review, corrected] }
        model:       { type: string, description: Model identifier and version pinned for this decision }
